cells.tense: You are at the work now, and your hands are on the adjustments.
cells.ask: Give the one project you keep circling back to a fixed hour today, same hour tomorrow, with nothing else in it.
cells.core: You add when it asks for more, pull back when it doesn't, and you are not doing it from your head. You feel the right amount and move. That is why the thing keeps getting better instead of just longer. It is a slow build and you are in it deliberately: not waiting for a sign, not grinding, because the repetition is where the skill comes from.\n\nYour subtlety is the only gauge in the room, so keep using it. Give the project a fixed hour today and again tomorrow, and let the rest wait its turn. What you are honing is the ability to tell what matters from what doesn't. That is what the hour is for.
cells.sheetLine: You feel how much the work needs, and you adjust to it.
cells.verb: keeping at the one thing until it goes deeper than you could have planned
cells.place: at the dial, adding and subtracting as the work asks

cells.tense: Something with a date on it is being treated as if it had to happen by tonight.
cells.ask: Set the work down at the end of today and spend an hour on something with a finish that is not the project.
cells.core: You are reworking, tightening, checking, and the dial has stopped reading the work and started reading your fear. When correction runs on urgency instead of touch, you grind the edge off what you have already built.\n\nThe steadier version has the depth arriving because you are not forcing it: steady passes, real gaps for rest, the work deepening at its own speed, and you still at the bench tomorrow. That is what the urgency costs you. Make something this month that is not the project — a meal, a tune, a row of stitches, anything with a finish, made where people can enjoy it too. The seriousness is allowed an hour off, and the hour is what feeds it.
cells.sheetLine: You are building against a deadline that nothing else shares.

cells.tense: Your hands came off the work a while back, and they have not gone back on.
cells.ask: Say the next concrete step out loud to one person, then do that one step today, crudely if that is what it takes.
cells.core: The adjustments stopped because no one is making them. You may be holding a picture of where the thing was going, holding it instead of touching the work again, and from a step back the picture looks more finished than the bench does.\n\nThe work is not beyond you; it just is not being touched. Put it back in front of you in the plainest way: one small move with an end you can see, done today. Do the crude version of the next step rather than the polished version of none. Small and real beats held. That is how the floor gets back under the whole thing.
cells.sheetLine: The work is fine. Your hands are the ones that stepped away.

cells.tense: The story says the work steered itself, and you made the calls anyway.
cells.ask: Name one thing you kept going this month as your choice, out loud, to one person who will hear it plainly.
cells.core: Which part to cut, what to keep, when to stop for the night — those were decisions with a decider, and in the telling they turn into luck, or into something the work did by itself. The settling of a piece, the moment it holds together on its own, still arrives through your hands at the bench.\n\nNothing about the practice changes if you claim it. The hours are the same hours, and the deepening came from what you chose to keep doing when stopping would have been easy. Say one of those choices out loud, like it belongs to you. What is already in your hands is the doing. What has not happened yet is the saying so.
cells.sheetLine: You kept this going. You keep calling it luck.
